text:
jia: quick heads-up — I'm prototyping a change to the dedicated-pool autoscaling policy focused on scheduling/eviction behavior. TL;DR: prefer small steady scale-downs that preserve KV/model cache hotness instead of large rapid drains. looking for ops + runtime tradeoffs.

matt: can you surface the user-visible problem you're seeing? e.g., is it cold-start latency, QoE regressions, cost, or capacity fragmentation?

jia: mostly two things: 1) big scale-downs (>=30%) are killing model KV caches and causing 2–8s per-request regressions for tail QPS (we see this on multimodel tenants). 2) Preemptive eviction for packable jobs sometimes forces pod reschedules that increase overall GPU utilization variance.

sofia: agreed on the cache hit impact. we saw the same pattern in canary last month — requests that hit an uncached KV for the first few tokens spike token-latency. current autoscaler only looks at GPU utilization and queue length. need a multi-signal approach.

arjun: what signals do we want to add? thinking: pending_queue_ms, 95p_latency, kv_cache_hit_rate, and a simple headroom target (free_gpus >= N). propose weighting them instead of hard thresholds.

autoscaler-bot: Notice: dedicated-pool/nyc-prod scaled down 12 -> 9 due to scale-down-window at 2026-03-04T12:14:07Z :warning:

matt: oof that bot message matches the incidents we traced. suggestion: introduce a "graceful drain" mode that attempts to retain replicas that have high local cache hit rate or recent model loads. eviction should consider per-replica metadata (last_model_load_ts, kv_cache_hot_score).

sofia: agree. also add a small cooldown that is adaptive: longer cooldown when kv_cache_hot_score > 0.7. otherwise short. we should also expose these metrics in Console as a per-pool heatmap.

arjun: rough policy sketch — pseudocode:
```yaml
policy:
  target_free_gpus: 2
  signals:
    pending_queue_ms: {weight: 0.4, target: 50}
    gpu_util: {weight: 0.3, target: 0.7}
    kv_cache_hit: {weight: 0.3, target: 0.6}
  scale_down:
    max_percent_per_5m: 10
    cooldown_base: 2m
    cooldown_multiplier_on_hot_cache: 3
  drain_policy: graceful
    allow_keep_replicas_with: [kv_cache_hot_score > 0.6, last_model_load < 10m]
```

eva: for experiments I'd run a canary on a non-critical tenant: compare current scaler vs weighted-signal scaler with a small max_scale_down cap (10% per 5m) + warm-replicas. measure 95p latency, cost delta, and cache-hit ratio. 2-week run with daily summaries.

matt: one edge to watch: eviction and scheduling interact with bin-packing. If we keep warm replicas, fragmentation can rise and we might need temporary burst capacity. recommend a burst-pool fallback to handle short spikes (30s-2m).

sofia: add one more constraint: when we detect a multi-model tenant (models_loaded_count > 1) weight kv_cache higher. that will automatically bias the autoscaler to be more conservative for those tenants.

arjun: implementation concerns: orchestration layer needs to surface per-replica annotations (kv_cache_hot_score) and accept a per-pool scale policy object. this touches the scheduler/apiserver boundary. we'll need a small API bump: PATCH /pools/:id/autoscaler-policy. also need to persist last_model_load_ts as part of replica metadata.

jia: noted. owners: arjun will sketch the API change, sofia will prototype metrics + console heatmap, eva will run the canary, matt will spec the burst-pool fallback. i'll draft an RFC with the pseudocode and experiment plan by EOD tomorrow and link it here: https://go/restricted/rfc/dedicated-warm-drain (placeholder).

arjun: one more thought — we should rate-limit scale-downs in terms of absolute GPUs, not just percent, to avoid tiny pools flipping too much.

jia: good call. add max_abs_scale_down: 4 in the draft.

eva: i'm +1 on experiment. can we include cost projection (per-hour delta) in the canary dashboard? that'll help PMs sign off.

matt: we'll also simulate worst-case (all tenants cold) to see the downside. put that in the runbook.

jia: thanks everyone. next check-in after RFC comments or Wednesday sync. :thumbsup:
